568.title: The second paragraph (Deuteronomy 11:13–21)
568.hook: what we do affects the rain and the harvest
568.howItsDone: The second paragraph of the Shema, Deuteronomy 11:13–21, is said morning and evening after the first; in some Reform prayer books it is optional or replaced, while Orthodox and Conservative prayer books include it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the whispered line after the Shema. Your line was some words are whispered. What did you say softly? Today, the Shema keeps going, into a paragraph about rain. Day five hundred sixty-eight.

The Shema doesn't stop at its first line, or at the paragraph after it: love the LORD your God with all your heart, teach these words to your children, write them on your doorposts. It has three paragraphs. The second one comes from later in Deuteronomy, and it sounds like a farmer's almanac with a warning label. Rain in its season. Grass for the cattle. And then a hard turn: what the people do reaches the sky and the soil.
screen: `THE SHEMA HAS THREE PARAGRAPHS.` → `A FARMER'S ALMANAC.` → `WITH A WARNING LABEL.`

segments.voice: It opens, in the old Jewish translation: "And it shall come to pass, if ye shall hearken diligently unto My commandments which I command you this day, to love the LORD your God, and to serve Him with all your heart and with all your soul." If you do, then rain: "the former rain and the latter rain," grain and wine and oil, grass for your animals. And if your heart turns away to other gods, the sky closes, the land gives no harvest, and you are lost from the good land. Then it repeats the commands from the first paragraph: these words on your heart, on your hand, on your doorposts, taught to your children. Three things stand out. First, the grammar. The first paragraph speaks to you, singular. This one speaks mostly to you, plural. It's about what a whole community does together. Second, the order. The Mishnah, in tractate Berakhot, explains why this paragraph comes second: first a person accepts the kingdom of heaven, and only then the yoke of the commandments. Third, the phrase serve him with all your heart. The Talmud, in tractate Taanit, asks: what is service of the heart? And answers: prayer. The phrase you met a few weeks ago, avodah shebalev, comes from here. The idea that rain answers obedience has troubled readers, and Jewish movements have handled it differently. The classic Reform prayer book left this paragraph out. Orthodox and Conservative prayer books keep it, and newer Reform prayer books often offer it again. Some readers today hear it simply: what we do, together, reaches the land.
screen: `IF YE SHALL HEARKEN DILIGENTLY.` · `YOU, PLURAL: A WHOLE COMMUNITY.` · `THE KINGDOM FIRST, THEN COMMANDMENTS.` · `SERVICE OF THE HEART IS PRAYER.` · then, large: `WHAT WE DO MATTERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: connect one action to its effect. Settle, and breathe. Think of one small thing you did yesterday: a meal you cooked, something you threw away, a word you said in anger or in kindness. Now follow it outward. Where did the food come from, and whose rain grew it? Where did the trash go? Who carried that word home with them? Follow it two or three steps, slowly. Notice how far one small action travels. The bell holds the time.
The second paragraph. Deuteronomy eleven, said in the Shema: rain and harvest tied to what a community does.
Your line: what we do matters. Today, choose one action with an effect you'll never see, and do it well anyway. Day five hundred sixty-eight.

569.title: The third paragraph (Numbers 15:37–41)
569.hook: the fringes, and the Exodus remembered morning and night
569.howItsDone: The third paragraph of the Shema, Numbers 15:37–41, is said morning and evening; in the morning, many people holding their tzitzit kiss them each time the word is said and look at them while reading.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the second paragraph, rain and harvest tied to what a community does. Your line was what we do matters. Which action did you do well anyway? Today, the Shema's last paragraph. Day five hundred sixty-nine.

People tie strings around fingers. They write on the backs of their hands. They set a photo as the lock screen, wear a ring, keep a stone from a beach in their pocket. Humans are forgetful, and we know it, so we hang reminders on our bodies. The third paragraph of the Shema is about exactly that: a reminder you wear. And in many synagogues, while it's being read, you'll see people lift the fringes they gathered earlier and kiss them, again and again, at one particular word.
screen: `A STRING AROUND A FINGER.` → `REMINDERS WE WEAR.` → `KISSING THE FRINGES.`

segments.voice: The paragraph comes from the Book of Numbers. God tells Moses to have the people make tzitzit, fringes, on the corners of their garments, with a thread of blue in each. And the reason is given right there. In the old Jewish translation: "that ye may look upon it, and remember all the commandments of the LORD, and do them." Look, remember, do. And then a warning: not to go wandering after your own heart and your own eyes. The eyes see things and the heart wants them; the fringes are a counterweight you can see. The word tzitzit appears three times in the paragraph, and many people kiss the fringes at each one. The blue thread, tekhelet, came from a dye whose source was lost for many centuries; some people today wear blue threads again from a dye they believe is the ancient one, while others wear all white. Then the paragraph ends with the Exodus: I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt. That's why this paragraph is said at night, too, even though fringes are a daytime commandment. The Mishnah, in tractate Berakhot, records an old argument: must the Exodus be remembered at night? Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah says he couldn't win the point until Ben Zoma read a verse: all the days of your life. The days of your life means the days. All the days includes the nights. So the Exodus is remembered twice a day, morning and evening, every day.
screen: `TZITZIT ON THE CORNERS.` · `LOOK, REMEMBER, DO.` · `NOT AFTER YOUR HEART AND EYES.` · `ALL THE DAYS INCLUDES THE NIGHTS.` · then, large: `REMEMBER TWICE A DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: kiss something meaningful. Settle, and breathe. Look around you, or in your pocket, or on your hand, for an object that carries a memory: a ring, a photo, a book someone gave you, a scarf, a child's drawing. Pick it up. Look at it, and let it remind you of what it stands for. Who gave it. What it asks of you. Then, if it feels right, kiss it, or press it to your heart, the way people kiss the fringes. Look, remember, do. The bell holds the time.
The third paragraph. Numbers fifteen, the last part of the Shema: fringes to look at, and the Exodus remembered morning and night.
Your line: remember twice a day. Today, look at your reminder once in the morning and once at night, and remember what it's for. Day five hundred sixty-nine.

570.title: True and firm
570.hook: after the Shema comes "true", affirming what was said
570.howItsDone: Right after the last words of the Shema, the prayer leader and congregation say emet, joining it without a pause, and the morning blessing Emet v'Yatziv follows; in the evening the parallel blessing is Emet ve'Emunah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the third paragraph, the fringes and the Exodus. Your line was remember twice a day. Did you look at your reminder morning and night? Today, the word that comes the instant the Shema ends. Day five hundred seventy.

A friend has just told you something big. You listened to the whole thing, and when they finish, there's a beat of silence, and then you say: that's true. Or: I believe you. It changes what just happened. Their words are no longer only theirs; you've signed your name next to them. The Shema has just finished: three paragraphs, from Deuteronomy and Numbers. And before anyone takes a breath, the prayer book puts one word right on its heels, so close that there isn't supposed to be a pause at all. True.
screen: `A FRIEND TELLS YOU SOMETHING BIG.` → `THAT'S TRUE.` → `NO PAUSE AT ALL.`

segments.voice: The Shema ends: I am the LORD your God. And the next word is emet, true. The Talmud, in tractate Berakhot, says not to pause between them. Tradition finds the pairing in the prophet Jeremiah. In the old Jewish translation: "But the LORD God is the true God." So the end of the Shema and the first word after it make one sentence: the LORD your God is true. Then the morning blessing carries on: emet v'yatziv, true and firm. And it doesn't stop at two. True and firm, established and lasting, right and faithful, beloved and cherished, delightful and pleasant, awesome and mighty, well-ordered and accepted, good and beautiful, is this word to us forever. More than a dozen words, piled up, all saying yes. It's a very old prayer. The Mishnah, in tractate Tamid, lists the words the priests said each morning in the Temple, and among them is emet v'yatziv. The Talmud even says that someone who didn't say emet v'yatziv in the morning, and its evening partner, emet ve'emunah, true and faithful, hasn't fulfilled their duty. Why so much insistence on this one word? Because, in the prayer's order, hearing isn't the end. The Shema says hear. Then emet answers: I heard, and I hold it to be true. That's the word's job here: not only saying the words, but standing behind them.
screen: `THE LORD YOUR GOD IS TRUE.` · `NO PAUSE BETWEEN THEM.` · `WORD AFTER WORD, ALL SAYING YES.` · `SAID IN THE TEMPLE EACH MORNING.` · then, large: `TRUE AND FIRM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say true to something you believe. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing you hold to be true, deep down. Not an opinion about the news. Something you'd stand behind: that kindness matters, that your child is good, that you'll be all right, a line of scripture, a promise you made. Say it to yourself in one sentence. Then, out loud, quietly, say: true. Notice what it's like to put your weight behind it. If doubt comes, let it come, and see what's still standing. The bell holds the time.
Emet v'Yatziv. True and firm: the blessing right after the morning Shema, answering what was heard with yes.
Your line: true and firm. Today, when you agree with someone, say so clearly, and when you say something, make sure you can stand behind it. Day five hundred seventy.

571.title: Who is like you? (Exodus 15:11)
571.hook: the Song of the Sea returns: "Who is like unto Thee, O LORD, among the mighty?"
571.howItsDone: Mi Chamocha is part of the blessing after the Shema in the morning and evening services; in many synagogues the congregation sings it together, and the blessing then leads toward the standing prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Emet v'Yatziv, the word true said right after the Shema. Your line was true and firm. What did you stand behind? Today, that same blessing runs back to the sea. Day five hundred seventy-one.

Twelve days ago we stood at the sea, with the Song of the Sea sung at the end of the verses of song. Then came Barchu, the light, the angels, great love, the Shema and its three paragraphs, and the word true. You might think the sea was behind us. It isn't. As the blessing after the Shema builds, it tells the story of the rescue again. Then it quotes one line from that song, and in many synagogues, everyone sings it together.
screen: `WE STOOD AT THE SEA BEFORE.` → `THE SEA ISN'T BEHIND US.` → `ONE LINE, SUNG TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: The line is from Exodus fifteen. In the old Jewish translation: "Who is like unto Thee, O LORD, among the mighty? Who is like unto Thee, glorious in holiness, fearful in praises, doing wonders?" In Hebrew it begins mi chamocha, who is like you. The blessing sets it up as a scene: Moses and the people of Israel sang to you with great joy, and all of them said, mi chamocha. A little later it says the rescued sang a new song at the shore, and quotes the song's last line too: "The LORD shall reign for ever and ever." Notice the shape. It's a question, but nobody's waiting for an answer. It's the kind of question you ask when you're amazed: who does that? Who is like you? The word translated mighty, elim, can also mean gods, and in the song's own world each nation had its gods; the song says none of them did what was done at the sea. There's a harder reading, too. A teaching in the Talmud, tractate Gittin, adds one letter and reads among the silent: who is like you, who sees suffering and keeps silent? It sits in the Talmud's account of the Temple's destruction, a reading born of grief. Both readings live in the tradition. And there's a later tradition that the Maccabees' name comes from the first letters of mi chamocha ba'elim Adonai. Others connect the name to a word for hammer, and the question is still debated. Every morning, though, the line is sung as it began: a question of wonder, from people standing on the far shore.
screen: `WHO IS LIKE UNTO THEE, O LORD?` · `A QUESTION OF WONDER.` · `ELIM: THE MIGHTY, OR GODS.` · `AMONG THE SILENT: A HARDER READING.` · then, large: `WHO IS LIKE YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask a question of wonder. Settle, and breathe. Think of something that amazed you lately: a kindness you didn't expect, a sunset, a recovery, a child's sentence. Don't describe it. Ask it, the way the song does: who does that? Let the question sit without an answer. If you pray, you can say the line in Hebrew: mi chamocha ba'elim Adonai. If not, keep the plain question: who does that? The bell holds the time.
Mi Chamocha. Who is like you: the line from the Song of the Sea, sung in the blessing after the Shema.
Your line: who is like you. Today, tell someone what amazed you about them, and let it sound like wonder, not a compliment. Day five hundred seventy-one.

572.title: No gap (Berakhot 4b)
572.hook: the Talmud says to join the blessing of redemption straight to the Amidah
572.howItsDone: In the morning and evening services, the last blessing after the Shema ends with ga'al Yisrael and the Amidah begins right away; the custom is to avoid any talking or pause between them, and in some synagogues the leader says the closing words quietly in the morning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mi Chamocha, the song from the far shore of the sea. Your line was who is like you. Did a line of joy get sung, even under your breath? Today, the last step before the great prayer. Day five hundred seventy-two.

A knock at the door of a palace. The king hears it, gets up, crosses the long hall, and opens the door. Nobody there. The visitor knocked, then wandered off to check something. The Jerusalem Talmud tells a parable close to this, about the king's friend who knocked and was gone by the time the door opened. It's a picture of a very specific mistake in prayer. You spend the whole service building up to the moment. Then, right at the threshold, you pause, chat, scroll, drift. Today, the rule that closes that gap.
screen: `A KNOCK AT THE PALACE DOOR.` → `THE DOOR OPENS. NOBODY THERE.` → `DON'T WANDER OFF AT THE THRESHOLD.`

segments.voice: The blessings after the Shema end on one theme: redemption. We've walked through them this week: true and firm, the song at the sea, who is like you. And the last blessing closes with the words ga'al Yisrael: blessed are You, who redeemed Israel. Then, immediately, the Amidah begins. In Berakhot 4b, Rabbi Yochanan asks who will inherit the world to come, and answers: the one who joins geulah, redemption, to tefillah, the prayer of the evening. A little further on, in 9b, the Talmud adds that whoever joins redemption to prayer in the morning will come to no harm all that day. So the rule is: no gap. No chatting, no stepping out, between the last word about redemption and the first word of the Amidah. In some synagogues the leader even says ga'al Yisrael quietly in the morning, so the room doesn't pause to answer amen. Why does it matter so much? Geulah comes from a root that means to redeem, to buy back. A go'el in the Torah is the relative who buys back family land or a family member sold into debt. So the order of the service tells a story. First you remember being bought back, at the sea. Then, while that memory is still warm, you stand up and ask. Thanks flows straight into asking, the way someone who's just been helped by a friend feels free to say: and one more thing. The bridge between them is meant to be seamless.
screen: `THE BLESSINGS END ON REDEMPTION.` · `BERAKHOT 4B: JOIN GEULAH TO PRAYER.` · `GO'EL: THE ONE WHO BUYS BACK.` · `FROM MEMORY STRAIGHT TO ASKING.` · then, large: `NO GAP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go straight from thanks into asking. Settle, and breathe. Think of one time you were helped out of something: a bad week, a debt, a mess you couldn't fix alone. Let yourself feel the relief of it again. Now, without breaking the thread, without checking anything, move straight on to one thing you need today. If you pray, you can say it as a request. If not, simply name it to yourself. Keep the two touching, like the last word of one sentence and the first of the next. The bell holds the time.
Geulah. Redemption, buying back. The theme the Shema's blessings end on, joined with no gap to the Amidah.
Your line: no gap. Today, the next time someone helps you, say thank you and ask your next question in the same breath, without drifting off in between. Day five hundred seventy-two.

573.title: The standing prayer
573.hook: the central prayer, said standing, feet together, facing Jerusalem
573.howItsDone: Jews say the Amidah at the morning, afternoon and evening services, standing with feet together and facing toward Jerusalem; it's said silently by each person, and in a congregation with a minyan the leader then repeats it aloud at morning and afternoon services.

segments.voice: Yesterday, geulah, redemption, joined to prayer. Your line was no gap. Did thanks run straight into asking? Today, the prayer it runs into. Day five hundred seventy-three.

At one moment in every Jewish service, the room changes. Everyone stands. Feet come together. People turn, quietly, all in the same direction. Lips move, but you hear almost nothing: a murmur, a page turning, someone's shoe. Some sway. Some stay perfectly still. For several minutes, a room full of people is completely silent and completely busy. This is the center of every Jewish service, morning, afternoon and evening. Its name just describes what your body is doing.
screen: `EVERYONE STANDS.` → `FEET TOGETHER, ONE DIRECTION.` → `A ROOM, SILENT AND BUSY.`

segments.voice: Amidah means standing. The Talmud often just calls it ha-tefillah, the prayer, as if there were no other. It's also called Shemoneh Esrei, eighteen, for its original eighteen blessings, though the weekday version now has nineteen. We'll walk through them, one at a time, over the coming weeks. The posture is part of the prayer. Feet together: the Talmud, in Berakhot 10b, connects it to the angels in Ezekiel's vision, where it says "their feet were straight feet." One straight line, as if you had only one leg, standing in one place. Facing Jerusalem: when King Solomon dedicates the Temple, he asks God to hear people who pray toward their land, toward the city and the house. So in New York, people face east. In Jerusalem itself, they face the Temple Mount. A blind person, or someone who can't tell direction, the Talmud says, directs their heart instead. And it's said three times a day. Berakhot 26b gives two explanations: the patriarchs set them, Abraham the morning, Isaac the afternoon, Jacob the evening; or they stand in for the daily offerings of the Temple. Both answers are kept. The idea underneath all of it, in the tradition's picture: the one praying is standing before someone. Not lounging, not walking past. Stopping, feet planted, facing one way, and for a few minutes nothing else gets the body.
screen: `AMIDAH: STANDING. HA-TEFILLAH.` · `FEET TOGETHER, LIKE THE ANGELS.` · `FACING JERUSALEM.` · `THREE TIMES A DAY.` · then, large: `STANDING BEFORE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand still for one minute. If you can, stand up now. Bring your feet together, side by side. Let your hands rest. Pick a direction and face it. You don't need to say anything. Just notice how different it is from sitting: your weight, your balance, the small work your body does to stay upright. If you pray, you can let this be standing before God. If not, let it be standing before the day. When the minute's up, sit, and keep breathing. The bell holds the time.
Amidah. Standing. The central prayer of every service, said on your feet, feet together, facing Jerusalem, three times a day.
Your line: standing before. Today, when someone talks to you about something that matters, stand up, or at least stop moving, and give them your whole posture. Day five hundred seventy-three.

574.title: Three steps in
574.hook: many step back and then forward before beginning, as if approaching a king
574.howItsDone: Many Jews take three small steps forward before beginning the Amidah, often stepping back first to make room, and at the end take three steps back and bow to each side before stepping forward again; customs on the opening steps vary between communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Amidah, the prayer said on your feet. Your line was standing before. Did you give someone your whole posture? Today, what happens in the two seconds before the standing begins. Day five hundred seventy-four.

A knock on a door that's already open. A pause in the doorway of a boss's office before you step in. People mark entrances even when nothing stands in the way. Before the Amidah, many Jews make one with their feet: three small steps backward, then three small steps forward, ending exactly where they started. If you didn't know, you'd think they'd forgotten something and changed their mind. But it's a whole entrance, compressed into six steps on a carpet. And it borrows its shape from the way people once walked into a throne room.
screen: `A KNOCK ON AN OPEN DOOR.` → `THREE BACK, THREE FORWARD.` → `AN ENTRANCE IN SIX STEPS.`

segments.voice: The steps forward are the older idea. Before you speak to a king, you approach. Commentators point to three moments in the Bible where someone draws near before speaking to God or to power. Abraham draws near to plead for Sodom. Judah draws near to Joseph, the ruler of Egypt, to plead for his brother. Elijah draws near on Mount Carmel before he prays. In the old Jewish translation, Genesis says simply: "And Abraham drew near." Three nearings, three steps. The step backward first is a later custom, and not everyone does it. The idea: you can't walk forward into a presence you're already standing in. So you make a little room, step back, and then come in properly. Halachic codes record the forward steps as a custom many keep. At the end of the Amidah there are three steps back again: the Talmud, in Yoma 53b, compares it to a student taking leave of a teacher, backing away rather than turning around. So the whole prayer sits inside a doorway: three steps in, three steps out. Notice what that does. Prayer doesn't begin when the words begin. It begins when you decide to go in. The steps are a hinge: before them, you're in your day. After them, you're somewhere else, in front of someone. Same carpet. Different room.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take three steps before something important. Think of the next thing today that matters: a call, a meeting, a conversation at dinner, a page you need to write. If you can stand, try it now as a rehearsal. Three small steps back. Pause. Three small steps forward. Feel the shift from wherever you were to where you're about to be. Then sit, breathe, and picture doing it, for real, just before that moment comes. The bell holds the time.
Three steps in. The small entrance many make before the Amidah, approaching as if before a king, with three steps out again at the end.

Your line: three steps in. A week that walked from the Shema's second and third paragraphs, through true and firm and the song at the sea, into no gap, the standing prayer, and its doorway. Today, take three real steps before your important moment. Day five hundred seventy-four.
